sections.h2: Does Minnesota tax a gain on a house sale?
sections.html:
Yes, when the gain is not wiped out by the federal home sale exclusion. Minnesota has four income tax rates for 2026, 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85%, and no separate schedule for capital gains. Gain is taxed as ordinary income.

A good share of Minnesota sellers owe nothing on a main home. Section 121 of the Internal Revenue Code shelters the first $250,000 of profit, or $500,000 for a married couple filing together, and the state's net investment income schedule leaves out any profit that is excluded for regular tax. Owners of rentals, second homes or recently bought houses face more steps. The sections below start with Minnesota's rates and add-on tax, then walk through the federal tests that decide how much gain is left.

These brackets cover tax year 2026, with returns filed in 2027. Indexing moved the thresholds up 2.369% from 2025 and left the rates alone. Married separate brackets are half of the joint ones.

2026 Minnesota income tax brackets
RateSingleMarried joint
5.35%Up to $33,310Up to $48,700
6.80%$33,311 to $109,430$48,701 to $193,480
7.85%$109,431 to $203,150$193,481 to $337,930
9.85%$203,151 and over$337,931 and over

Head of household and married separate brackets are posted separately. The 2026 standard deductions are $15,300 for single and married separate filers, $30,600 for married joint and $23,000 for head of household. These thresholds apply to taxable income, so a large gain in the year of sale can push the top slice of your income into the 9.85% bracket.

sections.h2: The extra 1% net investment income tax
sections.html:
Minnesota layers a 1% tax on net investment income over $1,000,000 for individuals, estates and trusts. On Schedule NIIT you subtract $1,000,000 from Minnesota net investment income and multiply what remains by 0.01. Corporations do not file it.

The schedule names capital gains alongside interest, dividends, rent, royalties and non-qualified annuities. Three details matter to someone selling a house:

  • Profit that is excluded from gross income for regular tax, like the main home shelter, never becomes net investment income.
  • Net gain on Minnesota class 2a agricultural land is subtracted out of the state calculation.
  • Estimated payment rules apply as they do to other individual tax, so an owner expecting a very large gain should raise withholding or estimates to avoid an underpayment penalty.

Partners and shareholders covered by a composite or pass-through entity tax still attach Schedule NIIT to Form M1 once investment income passes $1 million.

sections.h2: How much of your home gain you can exclude
sections.html:
The shelter is $250,000 per seller or $500,000 on a joint return, and the Minnesota schedule applies it to the state net investment tax too. Two tests must be passed. The owner, or one spouse, must have held title for 24 months inside the five years before closing. Both spouses must have used the house as their residence for 24 months inside that same span. Those months can be spread out, and the two tests may be met in different two-year stretches.

The IRS generally denies the shelter to a seller who already used it on another house during the prior two years. Extended-duty members of the uniformed services, the Foreign Service and the intelligence community may pause the five-year clock for up to a decade.

Only the profit above the cap is reported as a gain. A married couple filing jointly has twice the room a single seller has, so a profit that is partly taxable for one owner can be fully sheltered for two.

sections.h2: Federal rules that set the size of your taxable gain
sections.html:
Gain equals the amount realized minus adjusted basis. Basis usually starts with what you paid. Houses that were inherited or given to you follow other rules in IRS Publication 551, and a loss on a personal residence cannot be deducted. Owning for over a year makes the gain long-term. A year or less makes it short-term, and short-term gain is taxed at ordinary graduated rates.

The 2025 federal long-term rates for most filers top out at 15%:

  • 0% on 2025 taxable income to $48,350 for single filers, $96,700 for married joint and $64,750 for head of household.
  • 15% above those lines, up to $533,400 single, $600,050 joint or $566,700 head of household.
  • 20% on whatever sits above the 15% band.
  • Up to 25% on unrecaptured section 1250 gain, which comes into play for a rental where depreciation was taken.

A rental or other investment property sold at a loss is treated differently from a personal home. Net capital losses reduce other income by no more than $3,000 a year, or $1,500 for married filing separately, and the rest carries forward. A taxable gain can also require quarterly estimated payments to the IRS and to Minnesota, so run the numbers before closing. Check the current IRS thresholds for the year you close. Report on Form 8949 and Schedule D. A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale goes on the return even when the entire profit is sheltered. If the buyer pays over several years the installment method is available, and the shelter still applies.

sections.h2: Selling Minnesota property as a nonresident
sections.html:
For people who live elsewhere, Minnesota Statutes 290.17, subdivision 2 assigns income and gains from tangible property in the state to Minnesota when the owner does not use the property in a business. Residents are different: resident individuals' income is not allocated outside the state, so a resident reports the whole gain here.

An out-of-state owner who sells a Minnesota house, cabin or lot should expect a Minnesota return for the year of sale. For the net investment tax, part-year residents and nonresidents allocate the figure using Schedule M1NR lines 1 through 8. If you moved out of Minnesota before closing, the date of the move can change the filing, so call the Department of Revenue before you sign the closing statement.

sections.h2: Records to gather before you sell
sections.html:
Keep the closing disclosure from your purchase, the records of what you paid, and receipts for improvements, because those papers fix your basis. A smaller basis means a bigger gain, so missing receipts cost real money.

Set the paperwork out in this order. First, the purchase closing disclosure. Second, receipts for additions and major repairs. Third, the dates you moved in and out, to prove the 24-month use test. Fourth, any prior home sale where you claimed the shelter. A tax preparer can run the gain with those four items in a short meeting.

A cash sale does not change the tax math, since the gain is the same however the buyer pays. It does shorten the time between listing and closing, which matters if you need to hit the 24-month mark or finish a move before a filing date. Ask the closing agent for the final settlement statement right away, because the amount realized comes from it.

faqs.q: What is the Minnesota capital gains tax rate in 2026?
faqs.a: Minnesota has no separate capital gains rate. Taxable gain is taxed within the 5.35%, 6.80%, 7.85% and 9.85% income tax brackets. A 1% net investment income tax applies only above $1,000,000.

faqs.q: Is there Minnesota tax on a main home that qualifies for the federal shelter?
faqs.a: Not on the sheltered part. Minnesota's net investment schedule leaves excluded gain out, and profit above the cap is taxable income.

faqs.q: How many months of residence does the home sale shelter require?
faqs.a: Twenty-four months of ownership and twenty-four months of use, both inside the five years before closing. The two periods can be different stretches.

faqs.q: Does the Minnesota net investment income tax apply to all home sales?
faqs.a: No. It applies only above $1,000,000 of Minnesota net investment income and skips gain that is excluded for regular income tax. The tax equals 1% of the excess.

faqs.q: Must I report a sale if the 1099-S shows a gain I can exclude?
faqs.a: Yes. A 1099-S triggers reporting even when all of the gain can be excluded, on Form 8949 and Schedule D when those are required.
